extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English poetry; literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Expository lectures on what makes effective (or defective) descriptive and pastoral poetry, with comparative judgements of poets (Thomson, Cowper, Crabbe, Bloomfield, etc.). Useful for literary criticism and close-reading of poetic technique and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural genius versus artificial artifice
rubrics_metrics.description: His art is as naked and undisguised as his nature; the one is as pure and genuine as the other is gross, gaudy, and meretricious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise for spontaneity and natural feeling (Thomson): a poet whose feeling of nature comes unforced and conveys itself by 'mere force of spontaneous expression' is admirable. But lacking sufficient 'art to conceal his art' can leave the work exposed to faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of self-correction and disciplined craft
rubrics_metrics.description: He takes no pains, uses no self-correction; or, if he seems to labour, it is worse than labour lost. His genius cannot be constrained by mastery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even natural genius needs some mastery and revision; leaving expression to chance yields uneven results—brilliant passages beside vapid or worthless materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding bombastic ornament and empty allusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Fills up the intervals of true inspiration with the most vapid and worthless materials, pieces out a beautiful half line with a bombastic allusion, or overloads an exquisitely natural sentiment or image with a cloud of painted, pompous, cumbrous phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (satirised): 'shower of roses' image. Critical anti-pattern: ornamental language that smothers natural sentiment rather than enhancing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describing the whole vivid impression rather than minutiae
rubrics_metrics.description: He does not go into the minutia of a landscape, but describes the vivid impression which the whole makes upon his own imagination; and thus transfers the same unbroken, unimpaired impression to the imagination of his readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective descriptive poetry often conveys the overall atmosphere and effect (colours 'wet and breathing') rather than cataloguing trivial details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multisensory description (beyond the eye)
rubrics_metrics.description: He describes not to the eye alone, but to the other senses, and to the whole man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good description evokes humidity, clearness, heat, cold, sound and tactile impressions — transporting reader into the scene (e.g., hearing snow drifting, feeling hearth fire).

rubrics_metrics.name: Giving a moral sense to nature
rubrics_metrics.description: It is thus that Thomson always gives a moral sense to nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nature-scene description can carry moral or reflective weight; moral reflection integrated into description is a valued quality in these poets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical qualities and cadence of blank verse
rubrics_metrics.description: Thomson's blank verse is not harsh, or utterly untuneable; but it is heavy and monotonous; it seems always labouring up-hill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blank verse should be tuneful and varied; heaviness and monotony are faults even when lines are not 'harsh'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of misleading anthologising
rubrics_metrics.description: Selections which have been made from his works in Enfield's Speaker, and other books of extracts, do not convey the most favourable idea of his genius or taste; such as Palemon and Lavinia, Damon and Musidora, Celadon and Amelia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anthology extracts can misrepresent an author's strengths or weaknesses; judge an author on integrated works, not only on stitched-together passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone must suit subject (appropriate indignation or restraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: His poem on Liberty is not equally good: his Muse was too easy and good-natured for the subject, which required as much indignation against unjust and arbitrary power, as complacency in the constitutional monarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match poetic tone/energy to subject matter; subjects demanding passion (e.g., liberty vs. tyranny) need intensity ('spleen is the soul of patriotism').

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to enter into others' passions for dramatic writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The author could not, or would not, put himself out of his way, to enter into the situations and passions of others, particularly of a tragic kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For drama and tragedy, a poet/playwright must empathise and convincingly inhabit others' emotions; failure leads to plays that are not acted or felt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity, precision, and careful choice of topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Cowper had some advantages ... particularly in simplicity of style, in a certain precision and minuteness of graphical description, and in a more careful and leisurely choice of such topics only as his genius and peculiar habits of mind prompted him to treat of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity and carefully chosen, precise detail can be virtues: they produce intimate, well-observed domestic and natural pictures (e.g., Cowper's domestic scenes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish versus fertile genius (balance of taste and force)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Cowper had a more polished taste, Thomson had, beyond comparison, a more fertile genius, more impulsive force, a more entire forgetfulness of himself in his subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically weigh polish (taste, restraint) against raw imaginative fertility; different strengths produce different kinds of excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding finicalness and over-fastidiousness
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an effeminacy about him, which shrinks from and repels common and hearty sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over-refinement or timidity in manner can prevent wide sympathy; writers should avoid a manner that seems 'fashionable' rather than genuinely human.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence and order in collected pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: Every one of these may be considered as distinct studies, or highly finished cabinet-pieces, arranged without order or coherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even excellent individual studies benefit from coherence and ordering; a collection of 'cabinet-pieces' should be integrated to avoid feeling fragmented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire: pointedness, force, and moral indignation
rubrics_metrics.description: His satire is also excellent. It is pointed and forcible, with the polished manners of the gentleman, and the honest indignation of the virtuous man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good satire combines polish of manner with genuine moral force and indignation; it should be both tasteful and sharply critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious poetry requires elevation and fire
rubrics_metrics.description: His religious poetry, except where it takes a tincture of controversial heat, wants elevation and fire. His Muse had not a seraph's wing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious or visionary themes demand a loftier, more inspired tone; purely decorous description of sacred subjects is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original genius needs education and cultural materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Original genius alone, without education, in modern and more artificial periods, [cannot produce] the same bold and independent results as in former periods ... original genius alone is not sufficient to produce the highest excellence, without a corresponding state of manners, passions, and religious belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context, education, cultural resources, and available materials shape a poet's capacity to achieve highest excellence; genius in isolation often falls short.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastoral suitability depends on national manners and climate
rubrics_metrics.description: We have few good pastorals in the language. Our manners are not Arcadian; our climate is not an eternal spring; our age is not the age of gold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pastoral poetry must resonate with a nation's character and environment; mismatch between pastoral ideals and national reality weakens the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of excessive literalness and petty detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Crabbe exhibits the smallest circumstances of the smallest things ... He gives the very costume of meanness; the nonessentials of every trifling incident ... Crabbe's poetry is like a museum, or curiosity-shop: every thing has the same posthumous appearance, the same inanimateness and identity of character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over-focus on small particulars can deaden poetry, producing a museum-like inanimateness; avoid making detail-substitution for life or feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best description may come from non-descriptive poets
rubrics_metrics.description: The best descriptive poetry is not, after all, to be found in our descriptive poets. There are set descriptions ... but none equal to those in Milton's Lycidas, and in the Winter's Tale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality pictorial description often appears within larger imaginative or dramatic works rather than in poems explicitly intended as 'descriptive'; value cross-genre examples.
